title: Send refunds in the currency's own units

blocks.text: The acquirer's merchant portal now serves merchants outside the euro and dollar countries, and the complaints have started. A restaurant in Santiago refunded a dinner and the cardholder got a hundred times too much back. A shop in Manama says its refunds come out wrong, and a Seoul merchant says the portal shows every purchase with two decimals the won doesn't have.

Merchants type the amount to refund as they would write it on a receipt (`42.10`, `25000`), and the portal shows the amount of each past purchase. Finish the two methods marked `TODO` in `src/main/java/com/example/practice/RefundAmounts.java`:

items: `field4`: field 4 of the refund, for the amount the merchant typed in the purchase's currency. An amount the currency can't carry exactly is refused with an `IllegalArgumentException`;
`shown`: the amount of a past purchase as the merchant would write it, such as `42.10`.

blocks.text: When you're done, the issuer reads the amount the merchant typed, in every currency. About five lines in total.
The tests use other currencies and amounts than the lesson.

cases.says: a refund typed in pounds is sent as pence, and a past purchase in pounds is shown with its pence
a currency with no minor unit is sent without scaling, so the issuer reads the amount the merchant typed
a three-decimal currency is scaled by its own decimals, also when the merchant types fewer
an amount finer than the currency's smallest unit is refused instead of rounded
the conversion is exact: no amount loses a minor unit on its way into field 4
field 4 is shown with the decimals of the purchase's own currency

origin.section: 11.1. An Amount Counts Minor Units, and Its Currency Says How Many Make One

concepts: Field 4 counts minor units of the currency in field 49, so the amount is scaled by that currency's decimals, exactly, and an amount finer than the currency allows is refused.
